title: The $50 million offer
hook: A small DVD-by-post startup wants you to buy it. Do you see where this could lead?

profit.label: Profit
profit.hint: Money the video stores make today

future.label: Future
future.hint: How ready Blockbuster is for what comes next

intro.text: It is 2000, and you run Blockbuster, the biggest name in movie rental in America, with thousands of shops full of tapes and DVDs. Today, two men from a small startup called Netflix are coming to see you. Netflix rents DVDs by post, and it is losing money.

d1.title: The $50 million offer
d1.setup: The Netflix founders ask you to buy their company for $50 million. Your shops bring in billions of dollars a year, while Netflix has never made a profit. If you buy it, its losses become yours.
d1.question: What do you say?
d1.advisor: Fifty million is small money for us, but Netflix is small too. The real question is whether people will want their movies by post.

options.label: Say no, but build your own online rental service now, even if it loses money for years.
options.outcome: You say no to Netflix, but you put a small team on a website of your own. It loses money, and your store managers don't like it, but by 2004 you have real members online.
options.why: You saw that renting online could grow, and you started early. But building from zero was slow, and Netflix kept its head start.
options.better: Buy Netflix while it is cheap, and let its founders keep building it.
options.takeaway: In 2000 you said no to Netflix but started your own online service.

options.label: Buy Netflix for $50 million and let it run on its own, even while it keeps losing money.
options.outcome: You buy Netflix and leave its founders in charge. It keeps losing money for a while, and some of your store managers grumble, but the fastest-growing idea in movie rental now belongs to you.
options.why: For a company your size, $50 million was a cheap bet on the future. You bought the threat before it could grow into a rival.
options.takeaway: In 2000 you bought the small rival while it was cheap.

options.label: Say no. Protect your store staff and owners, and keep the money in what works.
options.outcome: You say no. As one Netflix founder later tells it, Blockbuster saw Netflix as a small niche business. Your own online rental service in America will not arrive until August 2004.
options.why: You judged Netflix by what it was, a small business losing money, instead of what it could become. That gave a future rival four free years.
options.better: Buy Netflix cheaply, or at least start your own online service right away.
options.takeaway: In 2000 you turned down Netflix and gave a rival four free years.

text.text: It is 2004. Netflix, now your company, is growing fast, while sales in your shops are slipping. Some store managers say Netflix is taking their customers.
It is 2004. Your shops are still the biggest in the business, but their sales are slipping. Your small website has members, and Netflix has many more.

It is 2004, and Blockbuster has more than 9,000 stores. But in the first half of the year, sales in your stores fell by about 5%, and renting DVDs online is growing fast. You still have no online service of your own.

d2.title: Fight Netflix online?

setup.text: Online rental is no longer a niche. Your website is small and Netflix is big, but you have something Netflix doesn't: thousands of stores.
Online rental is no longer a niche, and Netflix has a big head start. But you have something Netflix doesn't: thousands of stores.

d2.question: What do you do about online rental?
d2.advisor: Every dollar we put online is a dollar we don't spend on the stores. And the stores still make our money.

options.label: Keep the stores first, and spend the money improving them instead of building a website.
options.outcome: Your shops get a fresh look, but people keep moving online. A year later, with store sales still falling, you quietly start a small online service anyway, far behind Netflix.
options.why: The market was moving online. Improving the stores protected today's money, but left you behind as the market changed.
options.better: Go online with force, and use the stores to make your service better than Netflix's.
options.takeaway: In 2004 you bet on the shops while customers moved online.

options.label: Go big online, a little cheaper than Netflix and with no late fees.

outcome.text: In August 2004 you launch Blockbuster Online, about $2 a month cheaper than Netflix and with no late fees. In under a year it passes 1 million members, but it costs a lot of money to run.
You cut your online price below Netflix's and spend big on ads. Members pour in, but so do the bills.

options.why: Going online was right, but you played Netflix's game on Netflix's ground. You had stores Netflix couldn't match, and at first you didn't use them.
options.better: Go online, and give members something Netflix can't: your stores.
options.takeaway: In 2004 you went online, but copied Netflix instead of using your stores.

options.label: Go online and connect it to your stores, even though it costs more and takes longer.
options.outcome: You launch online rental with a twist: members can return their DVDs at any of your stores. It takes longer to build and costs more, but nobody else can offer it.
options.why: You turned your biggest cost, thousands of stores, into something Netflix could never copy.
options.takeaway: In 2004 you used your stores as a weapon online.

d2b.title: What to do with Netflix?
d2b.setup: Netflix is growing fast, and your store managers are angry. They want you to slow it down, so it stops taking their customers.
d2b.question: What do you do with Netflix?
d2b.advisor: If Netflix takes customers from our stores, at least it is our Netflix. But the stores still pay the bills.

options.label: Link Netflix to your stores so members can return DVDs in any shop, despite the hard work.
options.outcome: It takes a year of hard work and angry meetings, but now Netflix members can drop their DVDs at any of your stores. No rival can offer that.
options.why: You made the old business help the new one instead of making them fight each other.
options.takeaway: In 2004 you joined your stores to your online business.

options.label: Let Netflix run on its own, and keep the two businesses apart.
options.outcome: Netflix keeps growing on its own, while the stores keep shrinking on theirs. The two teams barely speak, and each sees the other as a rival.
options.why: Netflix was safe, but your stores and your website were fighting each other instead of working together.
options.better: Link Netflix and the stores, so each one makes the other stronger.
options.takeaway: In 2004 you let your two businesses compete instead of helping each other.

options.label: Slow Netflix down, and keep its prices high so it doesn't hurt the stores.
options.outcome: The stores get a little breathing room. But Netflix's growth stalls, its best people leave, and a new online rival starts to take the customers you held back.
options.why: You held back your own future to protect your past. Someone else stepped into the space you left.
options.better: Let Netflix grow, and use the stores to help it.
options.takeaway: In 2004 you slowed your own online business to protect the shops.

fees.title: Late fees
fees.setup: Customers hate paying late fees, and online services like Netflix charge none. But late fees bring in about an eighth of your rental money, and a big share of your profit.
fees.question: What do you do about late fees?
fees.advisor: Late fees make our customers angry. They also pay a lot of our bills.

options.label: Keep late fees for now. They pay for the online fight, and store customers still come.
options.outcome: The late fees keep coming in, and so do the angry customers. More and more of them decide that renting without late fees is simply nicer, and they don't come back.
options.why: You protected profit that customers resented, while your rivals used that anger to win them away.
options.better: Drop late fees, but test first and plan how to make up the money.
options.takeaway: In 2004 you kept a fee your customers hated.

options.label: Drop late fees in every US store from 1 January. It will cost a lot of money.

outcome.text: From 1 January 2005, your US stores stop charging late fees. Customers get one extra week, and after that they buy the movie. In the first three months, late-fee money falls by $128.5 million, and Blockbuster makes a loss.
Your stores stop charging late fees. Customers cheer, but the money they used to pay is gone overnight, and your profit falls hard.

options.why: Dropping late fees took away a big reason to leave. But you did it all at once, with no plan to replace the money, and it hurt badly.
options.better: Test it in a few cities first, and plan how to make up the money.
options.takeaway: In 2004 you dropped late fees, but paid a huge price all at once.

options.label: Try no late fees in a few cities first. It's slower, and Netflix won't wait.
options.outcome: You try it in a few cities. It costs less than you feared, you learn which customers come back more often, and you roll it out step by step, with a plan to pay for it.
options.why: You moved toward what customers wanted, but learned the real cost before betting the whole company on it.
options.takeaway: In 2004 you tested a risky change before rolling it out.

text.text: Your shareholders are not happy. An activist investor has bought a big stake, and he says you are spending far too much, most of all on going online. In May 2005 his people win three seats on your board. You keep your job, but now every dollar is watched.
It is 2005. The late fees still bring in money, but your stores get emptier every month, and online rental keeps growing.
It is 2005. Your late-fee test is working, and the board trusts your numbers. But Netflix is still growing faster than you.

d3.title: Use the stores as a weapon

setup.text: Netflix members can already return their DVDs in your stores. New online rivals are copying Netflix, but none of them has stores, and you could go further.
Netflix has millions of members, but new online rivals are copying it, and your shops keep losing customers. None of those rivals has stores, though.
Members can already return their DVDs in your stores. Netflix is still bigger online, but it has no stores at all, and you could go further.
In mid-2005, Netflix had about 3 million online members, and you had about 1 million. But Netflix has no stores, and you still have thousands.

d3.question: How do you fight back?
d3.advisor: Netflix can't open a store tomorrow. But every free rental we give away is money we don't make.

options.label: Cut online spending, and save the cash for the stores that pay the bills.
options.outcome: You save cash this year. But your online members drift to rivals, and your stores keep losing customers too.
options.why: You cut the part of the business that was growing to feed the part that was shrinking.
options.better: Use the stores to make your online service better than anyone else's.
options.takeaway: In 2006 you cut the future to pay for the past.

options.label: Keep online and stores apart, and spend more on advertising.
options.outcome: The ads bring in some members, but your stores sit there doing nothing for your website.
options.why: Advertising can't beat a rival that is already bigger. You had a weapon Netflix lacked and didn't use it.
options.better: Link the stores to online, so members get something Netflix can't offer.
options.takeaway: In 2006 you spent on ads instead of using your stores.

options.label: Let online members swap mailed DVDs for free rentals in your stores. It will be costly.

outcome.text: On 1 November 2006 you launch Total Access. Members can swap a DVD that came by post for a free rental in any of your stores, with plans from $5.99 a month. Members sign up fast, but it costs far more than you planned.
Members love swapping their DVDs for free rentals in your stores, and they sign up fast. But every free rental costs you money.

options.why: You finally used what Netflix didn't have, thousands of stores, to give members something better.
options.takeaway: In 2006 you turned your stores into a weapon.

text.text: It is 2007. Blockbuster lost over $4 billion from 2002 to 2005, and the free swaps cost a lot. After a fight with the board over pay, Blockbuster's CEO leaves, and a new boss arrives from 7-Eleven. From here, you play the new CEO.
It is 2007. Movies are starting to move over the internet, and your shops get quieter every month. Netflix is your fastest-growing business, and your shops are your slowest.
It is 2007. Your losses are big, the board wants them to stop, and people are starting to watch movies over the internet.

d4.title: Save cash or keep going?

setup.text: Netflix is still growing, but your shops are losing money fast, and investors want the losses to stop. Meanwhile, movies are starting to arrive over the internet.
Total Access is winning members from Netflix, but the free swaps in your stores are expensive. Investors want the losses to stop.
Your losses keep growing, and investors want them to stop. Meanwhile, movies are starting to arrive over the internet.

d4.question: What is your plan?
d4.advisor: Cutting costs is easy. Cutting the right costs is the hard part.

options.label: Make online pay its own way: charge for store swaps, and fund new store ideas.

outcome.text: You charge members $7 more a month for swaps in your stores, and you test new store layouts and small electronics. In summer 2007 Blockbuster loses 500,000 online members, and after a meeting with investors in November its shares fall 17%.
Prices go up, and online members start to leave for cheaper rivals. The new store ideas don't bring people back.

options.why: You raised prices on the part of the business that was winning, and spent the money on the part that was losing.
options.better: Keep online cheap, close weak stores, and invest in watching over the internet.
options.takeaway: In 2007 you charged your best customers more to save the stores.

options.label: Close hundreds of weak stores, lay off their staff, and put the money into downloads.
options.outcome: You close hundreds of weak stores, and thousands of staff lose their jobs. For two years the losses go on and investors complain, but when people start watching movies over the internet, you are ready.
options.why: You paid for the future by shrinking the past, before the market forced you to.
options.takeaway: In 2007 you shrank the stores to fund what came next.

options.label: Close half your stores, and keep online as it is. It saves cash quickly.
options.outcome: Half the stores close, and the losses shrink. But your online rivals keep pulling ahead, and you have fewer stores left to fight with.
options.why: Cutting costs bought time, but you didn't use the time to build anything new.
options.better: Close weak stores, and put the savings into watching over the internet.
options.takeaway: In 2007 you cut costs but built nothing new.

text.text: Netflix grows into the way millions of people watch movies, and it belongs to Blockbuster. The shops shrink, but the company lives on in a new form.
You moved before the stores ran out of road. Blockbuster becomes a name people use to watch movies at home over the internet, not just a shop at the mall.

survivor.title: Smaller, but still here
survivor.text: Blockbuster is much smaller, with fewer stores and an online business that never quite catches Netflix. But it survives, and it still has a place on movie night.

text.text: Blockbuster never recovers. In July 2010 the New York Stock Exchange stops trading its shares, and in September it files for bankruptcy, with 3,000 US stores still open. In April 2011 DISH Network buys what is left for about $320 million.
The stores empty out, and the online business is too small to save you. Blockbuster sinks under its debts, and its pieces are sold off.

fired.title: The board lets you go
fired.text: Three costly calls are too many. The board, tired of falling sales and lost customers, gives your job to someone else.

realHistory: In 2000 Blockbuster said no to buying Netflix for $50 million. It started its own online DVD rental only in 2004, ended late fees in 2005, and in 2006 let online members swap DVDs in its stores. In 2007 a new CEO charged extra for those swaps, and members left. In 2010 Blockbuster went bankrupt, and in 2011 DISH Network bought what was left for about $320 million.
